title: Back-Rank Checkmate
hintText: Look at Black's back rank. Their King is trapped behind their own pawns.

explanation.blunder: Black neglected to push h6 or g6 to give their King a retreat square ('luft').
explanation.takeaway: Always keep an eye on unprotected back ranks. A single major piece can deliver instant mate if the king has no escape.

title: Decisive Overload
hintText: Black has one rook guarding e8. Can you overload or deflect it?

explanation.blunder: Black relied on a single rook on a8 to defend against both the Queen and the Rook.
explanation.takeaway: When a defending piece has more than one obligation, a sacrifice can drag it away, allowing your second attacker to deliver mate.

title: The Royal Knight Fork
hintText: Your knight can jump to a square that attacks both the King and the unprotected rook.

explanation.blunder: Black left the c8-rook unprotected while their King sat on g8 without escape from e7 checks.
explanation.takeaway: Knights are dangerous leapers. Whenever an enemy piece is undefended, calculate if a knight check can simultaneously attack it.

title: Absolute Rook Skewer
hintText: Can you check the King along an open file where the enemy rook is directly behind it?

explanation.blunder: Black lined up their valuable King directly in front of their undefended Rook on the e-file.
explanation.takeaway: A skewer attacks a more valuable piece (the King) that must move, leaving the piece behind it exposed to capture.

title: Morphy's Opera Deflection (1858)
hintText: The d7 knight is the only piece stopping Rd8 mate. How do you remove or deflect it?

explanation.blunder: Black left their King stuck in the center without castling, guarded only by the knight on d7.
explanation.takeaway: Paul Morphy demonstrated that time and development trump material. Sacrificing the Queen to remove the defender ends the game immediately.

title: Boden's Mate Theme
hintText: Look at the criss-crossing bishop diagonals towards Black's queenside King.

explanation.blunder: Black's c6 and d7 pawns blocked their own king's flight paths, while two enemy bishops dominated the diagonals.
explanation.takeaway: Pairs of bishops cutting across an open king's position are deadly. Sacrificing a queen on c6 completely breaks open the diagonal for Ba6#.

title: Philidor's Smothered Mate
hintText: Force Black's own rook to surround and trap its King.

explanation.blunder: Black allowed White's knight to control the f7 escape square while the Queen aimed directly at g8.
explanation.takeaway: When an enemy king is hemmed in by its own pawns, sacrifice your queen with check to force their rook to block the king's last exit, setting up a knight mate.

title: Anastasia's Mate
hintText: The knight on e7 walls off g8 and g6. How do you open the h-file for your rook?

explanation.blunder: Black gave up the e7 outpost to White's knight, which created a lethal barrier trapping the King against the board edge.
explanation.takeaway: Knight on e7 + open h-file rook is an unstoppable checkmate pattern. Sacrificing the Queen to pry open the file finishes the combination.

title: The Immortal Game (Anderssen vs Kieseritzky, 1851)
hintText: Anderssen famously offered his Queen as the ultimate decoy to deliver checkmate with his two remaining bishops.

explanation.concept: Ultimate Queen Decoy into Minor Piece Mate
explanation.blunder: Black went on a reckless Queen hunt gobbling both White rooks on a1 and h1, leaving their own King surrounded.
explanation.takeaway: Material is secondary to coordinated mating threats. Sacrificing the Queen on f6 removes the knight guarding e7, allowing Be7#.

title: Game of the Century (Bobby Fischer vs Donald Byrne, 1956)
hintText: Playing as 13-year-old Bobby Fischer: ignore the attack on your Queen and offer it with 17...Be6!!

explanation.blunder: White attacked the Black Queen expecting an easy retreat, underestimating Black's crushing bishop discovered checks.
explanation.takeaway: Bobby Fischer's 17...Be6!! is one of the most famous moves in chess history, launching a decisive windmill that dismantled White's entire army.

title: The Gold Coins Game (Marshall vs Levitsky, 1912)
hintText: Frank Marshall placed his Queen where THREE different White pieces could capture it!

explanation.blunder: White moved Rc5 trying to counter-attack Black's Queen, failing to see the mate threats on h2 and f2.
explanation.takeaway: 23...Qg3!! provoked spectators to shower the board with gold coins. If 24.hxg3 Ne2#, if 24.fxg3 Ne2+ 25.Kh1 Rxf1#, and if 24.Qxg3 Ne2+ forks and wins.

title: Carlsen's Championship Queen Sac (vs Karjakin, 2016)
hintText: Karjakin threatens mate on g2 and f1. Can you sacrifice your Queen to force mate first?

explanation.concept: Decoy Queen Sacrifice on the Edge
explanation.blunder: Black sought counterplay with 49...Kh7, hoping their active queen and rook would provide perpetual checks.
explanation.takeaway: Magnus Carlsen won his World Championship tiebreak with 50.Qh6+!! Both 50...Kxh6 51.Rh8# and 50...gxh6 51.Rxf7# deliver unavoidable checkmate.

title: Lasker's Double Bishop Sacrifice (1889)
hintText: World Champion Emanuel Lasker destroyed Black's kingside by sacrificing BOTH bishops sequentially.

explanation.blunder: Black played passively with their pieces on the queenside, leaving the King unprotected against light and dark bishop breaches.
explanation.takeaway: The double bishop sacrifice (Bxh7+ followed by Bxg7) strips the enemy King naked, followed by Qh5+ and a lethal rook lift via Rf3-h3.

title: Kasparov's Immortal (vs Topalov, 1999)
hintText: Kasparov initiated one of the greatest attacking combinations in history with a legendary rook sacrifice on d4.

explanation.concept: The Immortal Rook Sacrifice & King Hunt
explanation.blunder: Topalov accepted the pawn exchange on d4, walking into an open d- and e-file double rook assault.
explanation.takeaway: Kasparov's 24.Rxd4!! dragged the enemy King all the way from a7 down to a4 in a breathtaking 15-move tactical pursuit.

title: Légal's Mate (De Légal vs Saint-Brie, 1750)
hintText: Your Queen is pinned by Black's bishop on g4. Is the pin really absolute?

explanation.blunder: Black pinned White's f3 knight to the Queen, assuming White was forbidden from moving it.
explanation.takeaway: Never blindly assume a relative pin is unbreakable. White gives up the Queen to deliver a stunning 3-piece checkmate with Bxf7+ and Nd5#.

title: Judit Polgár's Olympiad Queen Sac (1988)
hintText: 12-year-old Judit Polgár saw that Black's back-rank rook was the only barrier stopping checkmate.

explanation.concept: Deflection Queen Sacrifice into Back-Rank Mate
explanation.blunder: Black relied on 16...Qf5 to defend the f7 and g7 squares, missing the direct Queen destruction of f8.
explanation.takeaway: Judit Polgár removed the defensive linchpin with 17.Qxf8+! After Kxf8, Bh6+ forces the king back to g8 for Re8#.

title: Alekhine's French Miniature (1931)
hintText: Notice how the a3-bishop controls f8 and the light squares. How can you expose Black's King?

explanation.blunder: Black played 9...b6 without castling, fatally weakening the e6 square.
explanation.takeaway: Alexander Alekhine struck with 10.Qxe6+!! After fxe6, White delivers Bg6# because Ba3 cuts off the King's escape to f8.

title: Capablanca's Deflection (vs Fonaroff, 1918)
hintText: Capablanca uses an intermediate check to decoy the enemy King, then unleashes a back-rank deflection.

explanation.blunder: Black placed their bishop on e5 expecting a queen trade, ignoring the overloaded f7 pawn.
explanation.takeaway: Capablanca systematically peeled off defenders: 20.Nh6+ Kh8 21.Qxe5! Qxe5 22.Nxf7+! fork forces the rook away, leaving d8 undefended.

title: The Siberian Trap (Smith-Morra Gambit)
hintText: Jump your knight into the center to deflect White's f3 knight from defending h2.

explanation.blunder: White pushed 9.h3 hoping to kick the g4 knight, ignoring Black's queen and knight battery aimed at h2.
explanation.takeaway: 9...Nd4! attacks the white Queen while simultaneously threatening Qh2#. If White captures 10.Nxd4, 10...Qh2# is instant mate.

title: Blackburne Shilling Smothered Mate
hintText: The White bishop on e2 is pinned to the King by your Queen. Can you jump a knight into the heart of their camp?

explanation.blunder: White blocked check with 7.Be2, leaving the bishop immobilized by Black's e4 Queen.
explanation.takeaway: A pinned piece cannot move or capture. Black's knight hops to f3 delivering checkmate, as 8.Bxf3 is strictly illegal.

title: The Halosar Trap (Blackmar-Diemer)
hintText: Black's Queen and bishop are targeting your Queen. Threaten something even more lethal on c7!

explanation.blunder: Black greedily took the Queen with 8...Bxf3, unaware of the unstoppable mate on c7.
explanation.takeaway: Checkmate ends the game. 8.Nb5! threatens 9.Nxc7# instantly; Black captures White's Queen, but 9.Nxc7# ends the game on the spot.

title: The Windmill (Torre vs Lasker, 1925)
hintText: Carlos Torre placed his bishop on f6, inviting Lasker to take the Queen and initiating the famous windmill.

explanation.blunder: Black's Queen accepted the White Queen on h5, stepping into a perpetual discovered check conveyor belt.
explanation.takeaway: The windmill is one of chess's most devastating geometries: alternate discovered checks paralyze the enemy king while cleaning off the board.

title: Réti's Double Check Mate (vs Tartakower, 1910)
hintText: Sacrifice your Queen on d8 to draw the Black King into a double check from bishop and rook.

explanation.blunder: Black captured 8...Nxe4 with an uncastled King exposed on the open d-file.
explanation.takeaway: 9.Qd8+!! forces Kxd8, leading to 10.Bg5+!! When in double check, the king MUST move — Black cannot block or capture, ending in 11.Bd8#.

title: The Polish Immortal (Najdorf vs Glücksberg, 1929)
hintText: Playing as Miguel Najdorf: sacrifice your bishop and knight to lure the enemy King into an inescapable pawn mating net.

explanation.concept: King Hunt & Four Minor Piece Sacrifices
explanation.blunder: White king walked out into the center expecting to survive, completely trapped in Black's mating web.
explanation.takeaway: Najdorf sacrificed all four minor pieces in this game. 20...Bg4+! 21.Kxg4 Ne5+! 22.fxe5 h5# delivers a breathtaking pawn checkmate.

title: The Epaulette Checkmate
hintText: Black's King is flanked on both sides by its own rooks, like shoulders with epaulettes.

explanation.blunder: Black placed both rooks on d8 and f8, blocking their own King's lateral escape squares.
explanation.takeaway: When the defending king's escape squares on both flanks are blocked by friendly pieces, a direct frontal queen check on e6 delivers instant mate.

title: Arabian Hook Mate
hintText: The knight on f6 covers g8 and protects the h7 square. Where should your rook deliver the final blow?

explanation.blunder: Black failed to defend h7 while White's knight occupied the dominant f6 outpost.
explanation.takeaway: The Arabian Mate is one of the oldest recorded checkmate patterns in chess history: knight on f6 shields the rook on h7 while sealing the g8 escape.
